title: Writing Shed
strapline: A cosy corner where writing has a real job to do.
intent: A dedicated, tempting writing space says loudly that writing matters here and is for everyone.
When there are real reasons to write — lists, labels, cards, messages, signs — children write because they want to, not because they're told.
Rich mark-making tools and surfaces build the grip, control and shoulder strength handwriting needs.
Playing at being a writer — an author, a shopkeeper, a postie — grows the identity of 'I am someone who writes.'
It's the place where names, letters, sounds and messages all come together with a purpose.
implementation: Set up an inviting, well-stocked writing corner — varied pens, paper, envelopes, clipboards, stampers, a postbox — and keep it beautiful.
Model being a writer yourself: 'I need to remember to bring the wellies — I'll write myself a note.'
Give writing real jobs across the room: a shopping list for the home corner, labels for the block models, a sign for the road.
Notice and value every stage — scribbles, marks, letter shapes, name-writing — as real writing.
Weave in names and sounds gently: 'That's the same letter your name starts with!'
Add a postbox and let children write and 'deliver' to friends and staff, then reply.
Follow interests — dinosaurs, superheroes, families — and stock the shed to match.
key_questions: What could you write, and who is it for?
What do you want your message to say?
What sound can you hear at the start of that word?
Which letters are in your name — can you find them?
Shall we post it — who will you write to?

impact.text: Children make marks and write for real purposes — lists, labels, cards, messages — and say what they mean.
Children write their name and recognise its letters, and copy familiar letters and words.
Children hold and use pens with a growing, controlled grip and steadier hand.
Children play at being writers — authors, shopkeepers, posties — taking on the identity with pride.
Children tune into the sounds in words and begin to link sounds to letters.
Children talk about their writing and read their messages back to others.

enhancements: A wide choice of pens, pencils, crayons, chalk and mark-makers, and varied papers.
Envelopes, a postbox and address labels for writing and delivering letters.
Clipboards to take writing out into the room and garden.
Name cards, alphabet strips and stamps for names and letters.
Themed writing kits linked to current play — a vet's notes, a builder's plans.
A cosy, well-lit corner made special with cushions and good display.

playing_exploring: Children choose to write, playing at being real writers with real purposes.
They explore all the different tools and surfaces for making marks.
active_learning: Children stay with a piece of writing because it matters to them and they want it finished.
creating_thinking: Children decide what to say, who it's for, and how to get their message down.
